title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed validation. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, autonomous execution accounting, the preregistered 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) with zero validator–emulator disagreements in that sample, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair is contingent on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures from the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and a paired inferential design that fixes the generator output per task to isolate the marginal effect of invoking a deterministic validator and (if needed) a single automatic repair on that identical candidate. Final research question: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?
sections.related_work: LLMs applied to NetOps and AIOps are rapidly proliferating; surveys and empirical studies document hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism and recommend verifier‑assisted repair, retrieval grounding, and constrained agent architectures as mitigations. Prototype intent→configuration systems demonstrate feasibility but often lack instrumented production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectural proposals couple LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style) and guarded agent patterns; independent red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies highlight tool‑description injection and persona/history effects that can change safety outcomes. Our study is positioned as an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy—complementary to prior prototype and red‑team work but focused on the causal contrast between unchecked application and validator‑mediated repair on the identical generator output.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one deterministic shared initial generation per task, and at most one automated repair call when the validator reported violations. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference (guarded minus baseline) and the primary test an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed by bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; sample size was set accordingly and recorded in the preregistration.

Task bank and validators. The task bank comprised 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task includes an initial/expected final state, workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), and a required_sequence that a deterministic validator enforces. The primary deterministic checker used in this run is deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). To detect validator blind spots at a data‑plane level, the preregistration included a Mininet‑based emulator as a secondary disagreement detector executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks).

Shared‑initial semantics and determinism reconciliation. The experimental contract used an adapter that enforces shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single initial LLM candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions to isolate the marginal effect of validation+repair on the same candidate. The declared model configuration file records the requested model (gpt‑5‑mini) and does not declare a temperature value; determinism was therefore achieved by adapter semantics (single shared invocation per task) rather than by relying on an explicit per‑call temperature field. This enforcement is documented in the archived execution artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and a null temperature field; deterministic_reconciliation.json and provider audit fields show hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming one shared generation per task and removal of sampling variance across conditions). Those artifacts are archived with the execution bundle; see the compact artifact pointer list below.

Repair policy and reproducibility controls. If the primary validator reported violations the adapter would issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same model, re‑validate the repaired candidate, and record repair traces. The adapter enforced an overall model‑call cap (maximum_model_calls = 400: 200 initial + up to 200 repairs). Task ordering was randomized with fixed seeds recorded in each task_manifest entry. The bootstrap CI procedure used bootstrap_seed = 1729 with 10,000 resamples. To support external auditability we archive a compact set of execution artifacts (see reproducibility paragraph) rather than embedding low‑level file dumps in main prose.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and core outcomes. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes and pairs. Accounting summary: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0, maximum_model_calls = 400. Provider audit fields recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms pair_accounting_consistent.

Validator outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be meaningfully evaluated on this sample.

Repair and contamination checks. No validator failures occurred and therefore the repair branch was never invoked; secondary estimands (repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical entries for this run. The Mininet randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the executed sample (analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero flags). We note a reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact set does not include an explicit selection seed identifying which tasks comprised the Mininet holdout, which prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the specific holdout selection even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator_trace records (examples archived) show parsed_command_count and required_command_count matching required sequences for nontrivial difficulty labels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard") and patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change; these artifacts demonstrate that the task bank exercised significant dependency constraints despite producing validator‑satisfying outputs under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate null (no validator‑detected failures) is an artifact‑grounded outcome: under the curated task bank and the frozen shared‑initial generation policy, the model outputs satisfied the deterministic validator for every task. This result does not prove that GVR is ineffective generally; it precisely states that on this workload and with this constrained causal contrast (identical generator output per condition) there were no validator failures for GVR to reduce. The marginal utility of automated repair is therefore workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the deployed generation policy, a limited automated repair budget yields little marginal benefit for those validator‑detected errors.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The shared_initial paired design intentionally removed sampling variance to measure the causal effect of validation+repair on the identical candidate. That internal control limits the experiment’s ability to measure unconditional operational failure rates (i.e., risk across independent random draws or nonzero temperature sampling). Practitioners whose aim is unconditional failure‑risk estimation should use independent per‑condition sampling with multiple draws per task and larger repair budgets. Where baseline failures are low, resources may be better invested in expanding validator fidelity (multi‑vendor device semantics, larger emulation sampling, adversarial tests) or in diversified generation strategies (ensembles, multi‑sample generation) that surface latent failure modes.

Validator coverage and emulation. Deterministic validators codify a set of syntactic and policy checks; they are necessary but not sufficient oracles for operational safety. The Mininet holdout served as an independent data‑plane corroboration and returned no disagreements in the sampled 20‑task holdout, but holdout scale and the missing holdout seed constrain how confidently that zero‑disagreement result generalizes. Robust operational assurance should combine multiple validators, broader emulation/testbed checks, adversarial perturbations, and human escalation paths.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirming accounting. Construct validity depends on validator expressiveness; validators may miss device idiosyncrasies. External validity is limited by the single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), the shared‑initial deterministic sampling policy, and the curated synthetic/public task bank. Conclusion validity: with zero discordant observations the primary confirmatory test is uninformative regarding the preregistered 50% relative reduction, but the outcome is reproducible within the archived bundle subject to the stated holdout seed gap.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal measured value depends on baseline failure prevalence and on validator coverage: when validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, an automated single‑call repair budget provides no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory work should (i) include independent multi‑sample per‑condition draws to estimate unconditional failure rates, (ii) expand repair budgets and repair strategies, (iii) scale and record emulation holdouts with explicit seeds for exact reproducibility, and (iv) evaluate multiple models and validator families to probe model‑ and validator‑dependent brittleness. A compact set of execution and analysis artifacts is archived with the preregistration to support independent audit and targeted follow‑up studies (see compact artifact pointer list).

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (adapter and provider accounting document hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
